title: Teaching Vision-Language Models to Measure Object Sizes from Visual Evidence
teaser: When a VLM says the table is 120 cm wide, it is often reciting the average table instead of measuring this one. Build a model that reads scale from the scene and falls back on typical sizes only when the scene gives no metric cues.
abstract: Vision-language models answer metric questions about object sizes and distances far better than chance, yet a single image is scale-ambiguous: a large room seen from afar and a small room seen up close produce nearly the same pixels. A model answering in centimetres must therefore combine class-size priors (chairs are around 80 cm) with the metric cues the scene actually provides, such as objects of known size, floor perspective or several views. Priors are not cheating, and humans use canonical sizes too. The failure is a model that uses only the prior and ignores the object in front of it, which standard benchmarks cannot reveal because real objects mostly have typical sizes. The goal of this project is a model that measures: its answers should follow the scene when the scene contains metric evidence, and fall back on typical sizes only when it does not. How to get there is open. Training on counter-prior data, explicit reasoning over reference objects, or geometric inputs such as depth are all valid routes, and the student chooses and develops one. Progress is measured on scenes where true sizes are deliberately atypical, for example rendered assets with known dimensions scaled away from their usual size, together with standard metric benchmarks, so that gains on unusual objects do not come at the cost of normal ones. The main baseline is prompting the model with reference objects.
milestones: Counter-prior evaluation scenes where true object sizes differ from typical ones, together with standard metric benchmarks
A method, designed by the student, that makes size answers follow the visual evidence
Evaluation against reference-object prompting: better accuracy on atypical objects without losing accuracy on normal scenes

prerequisites.label: Experience with PyTorch and running large open-weight VLMs
Basic Blender or rendering-pipeline familiarity is a plus
